content: Sudafed is a brand name and registered trademark for a range of over-the-counter (OTC) decongestants manufactured by Pfizer Inc. These products are available for purchase in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. The name Sudafed is derived from the active ingredient traditionally associated with the product, pseudoephedrine hydrochloride. However, due to legal restrictions on the sale of pseudoephedrine in many markets, some products sold under the Sudafed brand no longer contain any form of pseudoephedrine. In late 2004, Pfizer publicly announced its plans to introduce a new OTC product called Sudafed PE, which does not include pseudoephedrine. Instead, Sudafed PE contains phenylephrine, a different decongestant that has been used in formulations for many years. By late 2005, decongestants with other ingredients were to be completely reformulated to include phenylephrine, although the original Sudafed containing pseudoephedrine would still remain available. This shift was driven by existing and proposed restrictions on the availability of pseudoephedrine-based products. These restrictions were implemented in response to the role of pseudoephedrine as a precursor in the illicit production of methamphetamine, a highly addictive stimulant also known as crystal meth. Pfizer and its predecessor, Warner-Lambert, had explored at least two alternatives to the existing pseudoephedrine-based formula in anticipation of regulatory pressures from state authorities and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). 1. In 1996, the company began testing a patented decongestant ingredient referred to as minus pseudoephedrine. Animal studies reportedly demonstrated that this modified version provided sinus relief comparable to the current plus pseudoephedrine. However, the key difference was that minus pseudoephedrine could not be converted into methamphetamine. Despite its potential, Pfizer did not bring this new ingredient to market due to the significant cost and time required to obtain regulatory approval. 2. Pfizer invested $12 million in efforts to develop additives for Sudafed that would make it more difficult to extract pseudoephedrine from the product. This project was ultimately abandoned in 2003, seven years after its inception. According to L. Hendeles of the University of Florida, Phenylpropanolamine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylephrine are the most common decongestants. Although all are sympathomimetic amines, their efficacy varies. In particular, phenylephrine undergoes first-pass metabolism, which limits its bioavailability at currently recommended doses. While doses of 20 mg appear to be safe and anecdotal evidence suggests greater decongestant efficacy at this dose, phenylephrine's effectiveness remains a subject of debate. In Australia, Sudafed products containing up to 60 mg of pseudoephedrine are available either by prescription or through a pharmacist who verifies the purchaser's identity using a driver's license. The pharmacist checks the purchase history against a database to ensure the medication is being used for personal purposes. If a driver's license is not provided, the pharmacist may still choose to dispense the medication at their discretion.
